newsitem.title: USA: POLL--US growth seen modest, but not fading away.
newsitem.headline: POLL--US growth seen modest, but not fading away.

text.p: Despite a second-quarter dawdle, growth in the United States may gain some vigor in the second half of 1997 before easing back to more modest levels over the next two years, economists said in the latest Reuters quarterly economic survey.

Thirty-six forecasters at banks, securities firms and research institutions projected, on average, an acceleration of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth to an annual rate of about 3.0 percent in third-quarter 1997 from the 2.11-percent level forecast for the second quarter.
Looking two years ahead, the economists predicted GDP growth would gradually reverse its course, slipping to about 1.9 percent by the second quarter of 1999.
Stan Shipley, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc, said GDP in the third quarter of 1997 should easily outpace its tepid second-quarter growth rate this year.

"We'll probably get some sort of pick-up going on into the third or fourth quarter," he said. Shipley said third-quarter growth should get a slight kick from a reawakening in consumer spending, which makes up about two-thirds of GDP.
Robust consumer spending early in the year had fueled first-quarter growth to a lofty 5.9 percent, the biggest gain in almost a decade.
Entering the second-quarter months, however, consumers appeared to be spent, as evidenced by declines of 0.9 percent and 0.1 percent in retail sales for April and May, respectively.

Many Americans are feeling relatively wealthy these days amid a surging U.S. stock market, said Stephen Slifer, chief U.S. economist at Lehman Brothers. But Slifer said potentially big spenders, such as the ubiquitous "Baby Boomers," probably would refrain from cashing in their blue chips to fund a spending spree.
"Baby Boomers are more inclined to sit on their stock market gains and view that as something that helps them out towards retirement," he said.
With monetary policy on the restrictive side and fiscal policy still fairly tight, economists should not fear explosive growth on the upside, Slifer added.

Nevertheless, some experts said a near-term pick-up in GDP growth above the economy's reputed potential growth rate of about 2.5 percent to 2.7 percent, may be enough impetus for the Federal Reserve to take action.
On average, forecasters bet on at least one more rate hike sometime before the end of the year, putting the federal funds rate at 5.75 percent.
An upward move by the Fed would inevitably slow growth, said Robert Brusca, chief economist with The Nikko Securities Co International Inc.
"The (economic) slowdown isn't something that is happening (now); rather, the slowdown is something that is coming after the Fed raises rates," he said.
The Reuters Poll was conducted July 7-9.
